alt: Six boxes around a central circle labelled rhetorical situation: exigence (why now?), writer (who is speaking?), audience (who is listening?), purpose (what should it achieve?), context (where and when?) and message (what is being said?). Lines join every box to the centre and to each other.
caption: Describe the situation as a web: change one component and the others shift.

after: ## Why the situation matters more than the topic
alt: One topic, libraries, branches into a council report on library funding and a retired reader’s letter to the local paper. The report leans on figures and neutral phrasing; the letter leans on personal experience and direct appeal.
caption: Topic is only part of the message: the situation decides how a text is written.

alt: Four rows turn vague labels into precise descriptions of the Gettysburg Address: “people” becomes citizens at a cemetery dedication and newspaper readers; “a long time ago” becomes November 1863 during a civil war; “to talk about the war” becomes giving the dead a meaning; “the war” becomes the dedication of a national cemetery.
caption: Precise descriptions name who, what and when; vague ones would fit any text.

alt: A timeline: the council’s vote to cut library hours (exigence) prompts a letter, which aims to persuade the council to reverse the cut (purpose). Below, message is what the text says and purpose is what the writer wants it to do.
caption: Exigence is the trigger behind the text; purpose is the effect it aims at.

after: ## Worked example 1: the situation behind a speech
alt: Anthony’s opening sentence sits above four numbered boxes for exigence, writer, audience and context. A fifth step links two phrases to the situation: “fellow citizens” assumes the point in dispute, and “the alleged crime” uses neutral legal language to put the law on trial.
caption: Each component is tied to a detail, and the final step explains an effect.

after: ## Worked example 2: an unseen letter (written by Marlbridge)
alt: The retired bus driver’s letter, published in the Larkfield Courier, reaches a primary audience of councillors through direct address and a secondary audience of Courier readers who might add public pressure. Two boxes explain how the personal detail builds credibility and how the anticipated objection shows awareness of the council.
caption: Spotting a primary and a secondary audience separates a precise answer from a general one.
